newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya shilling slides, some foreign investors sell.
newsitem.headline: Kenya shilling slides, some foreign investors sell.

text.p: Kenya's shilling slumped to its lowest value since early 1994 and investors sold a record amount of treasury bonds on Wednesday because of sustained fears about politics and the economy.
A general strike called for Friday by an opposition-backed alliance demanding constitutional reforms compounded nervousness in Nairobi and the pressure on President Daniel arap Moi, 73.
A go-slow by air traffic controllers, timed to coincide with a busy tourist season, went into its fifth day and foreign airlines voiced safety concerns.
Central Bank of Kenya Governor Micah Cheserem appealed for an end to panic in the foreign exchange market as the shilling slid by 5.06 percent against the dollar from Tuesday's close.
Cheserem said the speed of the fall was causing concern as banks reported some importers rushing to pay their foreign bills while exporters were holding back selling dollar earnings.
"It is being reported by commercial banks that some foreign investors in treasury bills and stocks are in the market to buy foreign exchange to repatriate their investments," he said.
"The combination of the above forces has caused the current turbulence in the foreign exchange market," the governor added.
The central bank sold at least $10 million to shore up the shilling, which closed at a mean of 67.5 to the dollar.
Wednesday's losses meant the shilling had depreciated by 13.4 percent since news last Friday that the International Monetary Fund, citing corruption, halted a $205-million three-year loan to Kenya.
Foreign investors on the Nairobi Stock Exchange sold a record 400 million shillings worth of treasury bonds on Wednesday, buying hard currency and repatriating the money.
But the exchange index made its first gain in four days.
In neighbouring Tanzania, the local shilling strengthened against the dollar and pound sterling partly because of an inflow of capital from worried investors pulling out of Kenya.
Commercial bank dealers said investors were alarmed at Moi saying on Tuesday that Kenyans would have to become self-reliant and the IMF package was insignificant compared to Kenya's economy.
Moi has yet to name a date for elections which must be held this year.
On the industrial front, Kenyan air traffic controllers on Wednesday ignored a government order to resume work and said their go-slow since Saturday would continue until they won.
The controllers are demanding a 50-fold increase from what they say is pay of about $90 a month, plus benefits.
Foreign airline heads in Kenya expressed concern about the safety of aircraft being forced to circle above Nairobi and other airports for hours during the go-slow.
David Keary, general manager for East and Central Africa for Lufthansa Cargo, said he was considering cancelling a Boeing 747 freighter from Nairobi on Friday at a cost of some $400,000.

"We are strongly considering cancelling the Friday flight, I am worried about the safety already, but if the general strike takes off, usually the first thing which will be hit is the transport sector.

"The fire brigade, the meteorological department...all the essential requirements needed to handle an operation appear to be in jeopardy," said Keary, adding staff to handle the flight might not turn up.

An opposition-backed alliance has called marches on Friday in support of the general strike, raising the spectre of violence between police and demonstrators. Clashes in Nairobi and other centres in June and July rattled some investors and tourists.
Some Nairobi businessmen said they were considering whether to close on Friday because they did not want to risk the safety of employees at work if mobs of strikers took to the streets.

Some 30 opposition members of parliament said on Wednesday they supported the general strike and urged trade unionists to remove the head of the Confederation of Trade Unions for saying he would not defend anyone fired for missing work on Friday.
